verses.verse:
मूलाद्यन्तेषु मध्येषु क्रमादन्यस्य योजनम्।
स्पर्ष इत्युच्यते लोके तस्य भेदास्तु द्वादश।९९।
verses.text: Joining another [note], in order, at the beginning, the end and the middle of the base [note] is called sparśa in the world; it has twelve kinds.

commentary.text: That is, when one note is given prominence and, taking it as the mūla svara (base note), other notes are combined with it in a special way, it begins to take many forms, like conjunct letters. Learned musicians call this action sparśa (touch) or kaṇa (grace note). Mostly the notes that join with a note are its neighbours on either side. If their various forms are counted, there are mainly 12 kinds. Though more than 12 can also be made.

1 - Pūrvādisparśa: if the note before a note is joined at the beginning of the base note, we will call it pūrvādisparśa. For example, the note before 'Ga' is 'Re'; if it is joined at the beginning of the base note, that is, 'Ga', it will be sounded like this: 'Re Ga - -'.

2 - Pūrvamadhyasparśa: if we put that same 'Re' in the middle of 'Ga', then, dividing the time of sounding 'Ga' into four equal parts, 'Re' has to be placed between the first part and the third part, that is, in the second part. Its example will be like this: 'Ga Re Ga -'.

3 - Pūrvāntasparśa: now if 'Re' is joined in the fourth time-division of 'Ga', we will call it pūrvāntasparśa. It can be sounded like this: 'Ga - - Re'. If this is used in movement, this same end-touch begins to seem like the beginning-touch of the next base note.
4 - Parādisparśa: in the same way, the note 'Ma', which follows 'Ga', that is, comes after it, can be joined at the three places in turn.
5 - Paramadhyasparśa: joining [it] at the beginning, the middle and the end of the base note 'Ga',
6 - Parāntasparśa: there can be three kinds, 'MaGa--', 'GaMaGa-' and 'Ga--Ma', whose names are written in order.
7 - Pūrvādyubhayasparśa: if the preceding and the following [notes] are joined to the base note together, there can be conjunct forms such as 'ReMaGa-'.
8 - But if its order is reversed, we will call it parādyubhayasparśa. In sounding, their form will be like this: 'ReMaGa-' and 'MaReGa-'.
10 - Parādi samūlasparśa; their example: ReGaMaGa--- MaGaReGa---
Then if these are also begun with the [base] note, two more are formed.
11 - Mūlādyanekasparśa: 'Ga Re Ga Ma Ga-'. These very groups of many joined notes are also called mirkī or murkī.

12 - In this way the glory of the sparśas, taking its endless forms in svaraśāstra (the science of notes), spreads from classical music to folk music. These were the touches of notes on a note; now the touch of śrutis on the notes, which the learned call mīṇḍ (glide), is considered.
